records.greek: Τότε οὖν ἔλαβεν ὁ Πιλᾶτος τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ ἐμαστίγωσεν.
records.gloss: Then therefore took the Pilate the Jesus and flogged [him].

L.1: Then Pilate therefore took Jesus and flogged [Him].

R.1: So Pilate took Jesus and had Him whipped.

decisions.choice: Pilate took Jesus and flogged him: Pilate ordered it and his soldiers carried it out
alternatives: Pilate flogged Jesus with his own hands
decisions.reason: A governor did not wield the whip himself. Greek, like many languages, says that a person did what he had others do; the soldiers who go on to mock Jesus (verses 2-3) are the ones who carried out the order. The responsibility is Pilate's.

decisions.choice: flogged: beaten with a whip, a Roman punishment
alternatives: the flogging that was part of the sentence of crucifixion
decisions.reason: The verb means to whip or scourge. Roman flogging was a severe beating that could be given as a punishment on its own or before a crucifixion (Mark 15:15). In John it comes before any sentence is passed, and afterward Pilate brings Jesus out and says again that he finds no case against him (verses 4-6). It seems Pilate hoped the beating would be enough for Jesus's accusers, as Luke 23:16, 22 says he proposed ("I will punish him and release him"). John tells it in a single word and gives no details.

decisions.choice: then therefore: after the choice of Barabbas
decisions.reason: The two linking words tie this to 18:39-40: Pilate offered to release Jesus for the feast, and they shouted for Barabbas instead. So Pilate turns to another way of dealing with the case.

decisions.choice: had him flogged (B); had him whipped (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "had" so that no reader pictures the governor wielding the whip himself (meaning decision m1). Readable uses the everyday word "whipped".

records.heading: The soldiers mock Jesus

records.greek: καὶ οἱ στρατιῶται πλέξαντες στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν ἐπέθηκαν αὐτοῦ τῇ κεφαλῇ, καὶ ἱμάτιον πορφυροῦν περιέβαλον αὐτόν, καὶ ἤρχοντο πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ ἔλεγον· Χαῖρε, ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων· καὶ ἐδίδοσαν αὐτῷ ῥαπίσματα.
records.gloss: And the soldiers, having woven a crown out of thorns, put [it] on of him the head, and a robe purple they threw around him, \v 3 and they were coming to him and were saying, "Hail, the king of the Jews!" and they were giving him blows.

L.2: And the soldiers, having woven a crown out of thorns, put [it] on His head, and they threw a purple robe around Him,
L.3: and they kept coming up to Him and saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and they kept giving Him blows.

R.2: The soldiers twisted some thorny branches into a crown and put it on His head. They put a purple robe on Him.
R.3: They kept coming up to Him and saying, "Long live the King of the Jews!" And they kept hitting Him in the face.

decisions.choice: a crown of thorns and a purple robe: the dress of a mock king
alternatives: a crown meant chiefly to cause pain
decisions.reason: The word for crown means a wreath or garland, such as rulers and victors wore. Purple dye was costly, and purple clothing marked royalty and high office (Judges 8:26; 1 Maccabees 10:20). The soldiers dress Jesus up as a king to make fun of the charge that he claimed to be one (18:33-37). The thorns would have hurt, but what John shows is the mockery. Mark 15:17 also says purple; Matthew 27:28 calls the robe scarlet.

decisions.choice: Hail: the greeting with which a ruler was acclaimed, here given in mockery
decisions.reason: The word was an everyday greeting, but it was also the cry with which subjects hailed a king or the emperor. The soldiers come up one after another and pay mock homage, as if to a ruler (Matthew 27:29; Mark 15:18). The form with the article ("the king") is used here as a form of address.

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: a royal title for the king of the Jewish nation
decisions.reason: This is the title Pilate has used (18:33, 39), the claim the soldiers mock. "The Jews" here means the Jewish people as a nation, as in any royal title; the soldiers, who are Roman, mock both Jesus and the people whose king he is said to be. It does not mean the authorities. Pilate will set the same title over the cross (19:19).

decisions.choice: blows: blows with the hand, given again and again
decisions.reason: The noun means a blow, usually a slap with the open hand, though it can be a blow with a rod; it is the word used when an officer struck Jesus before Annas (18:22). The verbs "were coming", "were saying" and "were giving" are all imperfect: the soldiers did this repeatedly.

decisions.choice: Long live (R)
decisions.reason: Readable uses the cry that young readers know for greeting a king. Literal and Balanced keep "Hail", the usual word for acclaiming a ruler (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: struck him in the face (B); kept hitting him in the face (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where the blows fell, since the word usually means slaps to the face (meaning decision m4). Balanced shows the repetition with "again and again", Readable with "kept".

records.greek: καὶ ἐξῆλθεν πάλιν ἔξω ὁ Πιλᾶτος καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἴδε ἄγω ὑμῖν αὐτὸν ἔξω, ἵνα γνῶτε ὅτι οὐδεμίαν αἰτίαν εὑρίσκω ἐν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: And went out again outside the Pilate and says to them, "See, I bring to you him outside, that you may know that no case I find in him."

L.4: And Pilate went outside again and says to them, "See, I am bringing Him out to you, so that you may know that I find no case in Him."

R.4: Pilate went outside again. He said to the people there, "Listen! I am bringing Him out to you. I want you to know that I find no reason to condemn Him."

decisions.choice: case: grounds for a charge, a legal reason to punish
decisions.reason: The word means the cause or ground of an accusation, the basis on which a court condemns someone. It is not a word for moral fault. Pilate says this three times (18:38; 19:4, 6): Roman justice, in his own judgment, has nothing against Jesus.

decisions.choice: I am bringing him out so that you may know: the beaten man is shown as proof that Pilate has found nothing
alternatives: Pilate hoped they would pity him
decisions.reason: John does not explain how bringing Jesus out shows this. It seems Pilate meant the sight of the flogged prisoner in mock dress to show that the charge was empty and that he had been punished enough. Yet the governor who says he finds no case has just had him flogged.

decisions.choice: them: those outside the praetorium who brought the charge
decisions.reason: Pilate has gone out to them before (18:29, 38). They are the chief priests and their officers (19:6), with those who stood with them outside; John calls them "the Jews" in 18:38. They stayed outside so as not to become unclean before the Passover (18:28).

decisions.choice: says (Literal); said (Balanced, Readable); likewise in verses 5, 6, 9, 10, 14 and 15
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage.

decisions.choice: I find no case in him (Literal); I find no case against him (Balanced); I find no reason to condemn him (Readable); the same at 18:38 and 19:6
alternatives: I find no fault in him
I find no guilt in him
decisions.reason: "Case" carries the legal sense of the word (meaning decision m1); Readable says plainly what having no case means. Each level uses the same English each time Pilate says it, so the reader hears the repetition. Readable adds "to the people there" and "I want you to know" to make the short sentences clear.

records.greek: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔξω, φορῶν τὸν ἀκάνθινον στέφανον καὶ τὸ πορφυροῦν ἱμάτιον.
records.gloss: Went out therefore the Jesus outside, wearing the thorny crown and the purple robe.

L.5: So Jesus went outside, wearing the thorny crown and the purple robe.

R.5: So Jesus came out. He was wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe.

decisions.choice: wearing: still dressed as the soldiers had dressed him
decisions.reason: The present participle describes what he had on as he came out: the mock crown and robe of verse 2. Jesus is presented to his accusers in the costume of the mockery.

decisions.choice: the crown and the robe: mockery of a king, which John's reader knows is in fact a king
decisions.reason: Jesus has told Pilate that he is a king, though his kingdom is not from this world (18:36-37). The soldiers mean the crown and robe as a joke; the Gospel's reader sees the true king dressed up as a false one. John lets the scene speak and does not comment.

decisions.choice: went out: out of the praetorium to where his accusers waited
decisions.reason: The same verb and the same word "outside" were used of Pilate in verse 4. Jesus comes out of the governor's headquarters into the open place where the chief priests stood (18:28).

decisions.choice: came out (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable tell it from the point of view of those waiting outside, as verse 4 has prepared. Literal keeps "went".

records.greek: καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἰδοὺ ὁ ἄνθρωπος.
records.gloss: And he says to them, "See, the man!"

L.5: And he says to them, "Look, the man!"

R.5: Pilate said to them, "Look! Here is the man!"

decisions.choice: he says: Pilate is the speaker
decisions.reason: The last person named is Jesus, but Pilate is the one who speaks to "them" in verses 4 and 6, and the words present Jesus to his accusers. The subject is left unstated in the Greek.

decisions.choice: Look, the man: Pilate presents the beaten prisoner as no threat, in pity or in scorn
decisions.reason: The words point to the man before them: beaten, in a mock crown and robe. Pilate's aim seems to be the one of verse 4, to show that this prisoner is no rival king and not worth putting to death. Whether he speaks with some pity ("see this poor man") or with contempt ("look at this fellow") the words do not say, and both may be present.

decisions.choice: the man: perhaps more than Pilate means
decisions.reason: John's reader may hear more in the words than Pilate does, as with Caiaphas in 11:49-52. The Word became flesh (1:14), and Jesus has called himself the Son of Man (1:51; 12:23, 34). Some also hear an echo of Zechariah 6:12, "Look, a man whose name is the Branch", but the wording there is not the same. John does not draw out any of these, and the deeper sense is uncertain.

decisions.choice: And he says to them, "Look, the man!" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the sentence absent (a few early witnesses)
decisions.reason: A very few early witnesses, among them the first hand of P66 and some Old Latin copies, lack this sentence. Nearly all manuscripts have it. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Look, the man (L); Look, here is the man (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Behold" is no longer everyday speech, and the Latin form of these words, "Ecce homo", is known from art rather than from speech. Literal keeps the bare Greek; Balanced and Readable add "here is" to make a natural sentence. The footnote gives the familiar "Behold the man".

decisions.choice: Pilate (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ὅτε οὖν εἶδον αὐτὸν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται ἐκραύγασαν λέγοντες· Σταύρωσον σταύρωσον.
records.gloss: When therefore saw him the chief priests and the officers, they cried out saying, "Crucify, crucify!"

L.6: So when the chief priests and the officers saw Him, they shouted, saying, "Crucify, crucify!"

R.6: When the leading priests and the temple guards saw Jesus, they shouted, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!"

decisions.choice: the chief priests and the officers: the priestly leaders and the temple police who served them
alternatives: the people of Jerusalem in general
decisions.reason: The officers are the men who kept order in the temple for the chief priests; they had been sent to seize Jesus before (7:32, 45) and arrested him in the garden (18:3, 12). John names only these two groups as the ones who shout here. He says nothing of a large crowd.

decisions.choice: crucify: put to death on a cross, a Roman penalty
decisions.reason: Crucifixion was a Roman form of execution, used above all for slaves and rebels against Rome. In Judea only the Roman governor could order it (18:31). By demanding it, the chief priests ask Pilate to put Jesus to death in the Roman way, the kind of death Jesus had spoken of when he said he would be lifted up (12:32-33; 18:32).

decisions.choice: shouted: cried out loudly
decisions.reason: The verb is the one John uses for the shouts of 18:40 and 19:12, 15, and for the crowd who welcomed Jesus to Jerusalem with "Hosanna" a few days earlier (12:13).

decisions.choice: temple police (B); leading priests, temple guards (R)
decisions.reason: "Officers" alone does not say whose officers these are, so Balanced and Readable name their role (meaning decision m1), as at 7:32. Readable says "leading priests" so that "chief" is not taken as a single leader.

decisions.choice: Crucify him! Crucify him! (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has the verb alone, twice. Readable supplies "him", which the sense requires.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Λάβετε αὐτὸν ὑμεῖς καὶ σταυρώσατε, ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐχ εὑρίσκω ἐν αὐτῷ αἰτίαν.
records.gloss: Says to them the Pilate, "Take him you and crucify [him], I for not find in him a case."

L.6: Pilate says to them, "You take Him and crucify [Him], for I find no case in Him."

R.6: Pilate answered, "You take Him and crucify Him yourselves! As for me, I find no reason to condemn Him."

decisions.choice: take him yourselves and crucify him: a scornful retort, not a real permission
alternatives: a real handing over of Jesus to them for execution
decisions.reason: They had already told Pilate that they were not allowed to put anyone to death (18:31), and crucifixion was a Roman punishment. Pilate throws their demand back at them: if they want this, let them do it, for he will not. The verses that follow show that he did not mean it as an order or a grant of power.

decisions.choice: you ... I: both pronouns are emphatic
decisions.reason: Greek does not need the pronouns, so their presence marks a contrast: you may crucify him; I find nothing against him.

decisions.choice: case: grounds for a charge
decisions.reason: The same word as in 18:38 and 19:4 (meaning decision there). This is the third time Pilate says it.

decisions.choice: yourselves (B, R); As for me (R)
decisions.reason: English shows the emphatic "you" with "yourselves" and Readable shows the emphatic "I" with "As for me" (meaning decision m2). Readable says "answered", since Pilate is replying to their shout.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Ἡμεῖς νόμον ἔχομεν, καὶ κατὰ τὸν νόμον ὀφείλει ἀποθανεῖν, ὅτι υἱὸν θεοῦ ἑαυτὸν ἐποίησεν.
records.gloss: Answered him the Jews, "We a law have, and according to the law he ought to die, because Son of God himself he made."

L.7: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to the law He ought to die, because He made Himself [the] Son of God."

R.7: The Jewish leaders answered Pilate, "We have a law, and that law says He must die. He has made Himself out to be the Son of God."

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers who have just shouted (verse 6)
decisions.reason: John has just named the speakers: the chief priests and the officers. They now answer Pilate's retort. It is not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus and his disciples are Jews, and many in Jerusalem had welcomed him (12:12-13).

decisions.choice: we have a law: the law against blasphemy, Leviticus 24:16
decisions.reason: The law of Moses put to death anyone who blasphemed the name of the LORD (Leviticus 24:16). The charge is the one made in 5:18 and 10:33, 36: that a man claims for himself what belongs to God. Before Pilate they had so far called him only a wrongdoer (18:30); now they name a religious charge.

decisions.choice: he made himself the Son of God: their charge, which John's reader sees in a different light
decisions.reason: "Son" has no article because it comes before its verb, but it is the title: the Son of God. John's reader knows that Jesus is the Son of God (1:34, 49; 20:31). What is false in the charge is that he made himself anything: he does nothing on his own, and it is the Father who glorifies him (5:19; 8:54). Compare 5:18 and 10:33.

decisions.choice: according to the law (SBLGNT)
alternatives: according to our law (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "according to our law". The older manuscripts lack "our", and the sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: has made himself out to be (R)
decisions.reason: Readable shows that this is a claim they reject (meaning decision m3), as at 10:33. It names Pilate, since "him" could be taken as Jesus.

records.greek: Ὅτε οὖν ἤκουσεν ὁ Πιλᾶτος τοῦτον τὸν λόγον, μᾶλλον ἐφοβήθη, καὶ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον πάλιν καὶ λέγει τῷ Ἰησοῦ· Πόθεν εἶ σύ;
records.gloss: When therefore heard the Pilate this the word, more he was afraid, \v 9 and he went into the praetorium again and says to the Jesus, "From where are you?"

L.8: So when Pilate heard this word, he was more afraid,
L.9: and he went into the praetorium again and says to Jesus, "Where are You from?"

R.8: When Pilate heard this, he was even more afraid.
R.9: He went back into the palace and asked Jesus, "Where do You come from?"

decisions.choice: even more afraid: Pilate was already uneasy, and now his fear grows
decisions.reason: John has not said that Pilate was afraid before, but the comparative fits his efforts to be rid of the case (18:38-39; 19:4, 6). The word can also mean simply "very afraid"; the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: this word: the claim that Jesus made himself the Son of God
alternatives: fear only of a riot or of being reported to Rome
decisions.reason: John does not say why this frightened Pilate. Romans told stories of sons of gods and of divine men, and a Roman could fear having harmed one; Pilate may also have feared trouble from the accusers. His next question, about where Jesus comes from, suggests the first.

decisions.choice: the praetorium: the Roman governor's headquarters in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The word was used for a Roman governor's official residence. Jesus has been held inside (18:28, 33), while his accusers stayed outside.

decisions.choice: Where are you from: Pilate asks about more than a home town
alternatives: a question about which region he came from
decisions.reason: Where Jesus comes from is a question that runs through the Gospel (7:27-29; 8:14; 9:29-30). He has already told Pilate that his kingdom is not from this world (18:36). The reader knows the answer: he came from the Father, from above (3:31; 16:28).

decisions.choice: the headquarters (B); the palace (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the praetorium was (meaning decision m3), as in 18:28 and 18:33; Literal keeps the Roman word.

records.greek: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀπόκρισιν οὐκ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: But the Jesus an answer not gave him.

L.9: But Jesus did not give him an answer.

R.9: But Jesus did not answer him.

decisions.choice: Jesus gave no answer: perhaps an echo of Isaiah 53:7
decisions.reason: The servant of the LORD in Isaiah 53:7 is like a lamb led to the slaughter that does not open its mouth. Mark 14:61 and 15:5 also tell of Jesus keeping silent before his judges. John does not quote Isaiah here, so the echo is possible but not certain.

decisions.choice: his silence: he has already given Pilate his answer
decisions.reason: Jesus has told Pilate that his kingdom is not from this world and that he came to bear witness to the truth (18:36-37), and Pilate turned away from it (18:38). John does not explain the silence, but it follows that refusal.

decisions.choice: did not give him an answer (L)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the noun "answer" with "give", as the Greek has it; Balanced and Readable use natural forms of the same idea.

records.greek: λέγει οὖν αὐτῷ ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Ἐμοὶ οὐ λαλεῖς;
records.gloss: Says therefore to him the Pilate, "To me not you speak?"

L.10: So Pilate says to Him, "To me You do not speak?"

R.10: So Pilate said to Him, "Will You not even talk to me?"

decisions.choice: to me: placed first for emphasis, to me, the governor
decisions.reason: The pronoun stands first in the question. Pilate is struck that a prisoner whose life he controls will not answer him, of all people; the next sentence says why.

decisions.choice: Are you refusing to speak to me (B); Will you not even talk to me (R)
alternatives: You do not speak to me?
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show the emphasis on "me" by the form of the question (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps the Greek word order.

records.greek: οὐκ οἶδας ὅτι ἐξουσίαν ἔχω ἀπολῦσαί σε καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔχω σταυρῶσαί σε;
records.gloss: Not know you that authority I have to release you and authority I have to crucify you?

L.10: Do You not know that I have authority to release You and I have authority to crucify You?

R.10: Do You not understand that I have the power to let You go? I also have the power to have You crucified!

decisions.choice: authority: the legal right and power to decide
decisions.reason: The word means the right to act, and the power that goes with it. As the Roman governor of Judea, Pilate held the power of life and death over a prisoner like Jesus (18:31). John uses the same word for the authority the Father gave the Son (5:27; 10:18; 17:2), and Jesus takes it up in his reply.

decisions.choice: release ... crucify (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts put the two the other way round: "to crucify you, and ... to release you". The older manuscripts have the order given here. The sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Do you not know: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: The negative form expects agreement: surely you know this. Pilate means it as a warning.

decisions.choice: power (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "power", the everyday word, here and in verse 11, so that Jesus's reply is heard as an answer to Pilate's claim. Literal and Balanced keep "authority" (meaning decision m1). Readable says "have you crucified", since the governor's soldiers would carry it out.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Ἰησοῦς· Οὐκ εἶχες ἐξουσίαν κατ’ ἐμοῦ οὐδεμίαν εἰ μὴ ἦν δεδομένον σοι ἄνωθεν· διὰ τοῦτο ὁ παραδούς μέ σοι μείζονα ἁμαρτίαν ἔχει.
records.gloss: Answered him Jesus, "Not you would have authority against me none, if not it was given to you from above; because of this the [one] having handed over me to you greater sin has."

L.11: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over Me at all if it had not been given to you from above; because of this the one who handed Me over to you has [the] greater sin."

R.11: Jesus answered, "You would not have any power over Me if God had not given it to you. So the person who handed Me over to you is even more guilty of sin than you are."

decisions.choice: from above: from God
decisions.reason: John uses this word for what comes from God and from heaven (3:3, 31); compare 3:27, "unless it has been given him from heaven". Pilate's power over Jesus comes from God, not finally from the emperor, and it is given only for this hour.

decisions.choice: it had been given: the whole matter, not only the word "authority"
alternatives: the authority itself had been given
decisions.reason: The participle is neuter, while the word for authority is feminine. So "it" most likely means the whole situation, Pilate's power over Jesus at this moment, which God has allowed. The sense is the same as if authority alone were meant.

decisions.choice: because of this ... the greater sin: Pilate is guilty, but the one who handed Jesus over is more guilty
alternatives: Pilate has no sin at all
decisions.reason: Pilate acts with a power that God has given to his office, though he is still responsible for how he uses it; "greater" means that Pilate's sin is real too. The one who handed Jesus over did so knowingly, from his own will, and set the whole matter in motion. Jesus speaks of guilt in this one case, not of any group or people.

decisions.choice: the one who handed me over to you: most likely Caiaphas, the high priest
alternatives: the chief priests as a group
decisions.reason: The word is singular. Caiaphas sent Jesus to Pilate (18:24, 28) and had said that one man should die for the nation (11:49-50; 18:14), and Pilate has said, "Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me" (18:35). Others take it to mean Judas, whom John often calls the one who handed Jesus over (6:64, 71; 13:11; 18:2, 5); but Judas handed him over to the men sent by the chief priests (18:3), not to Pilate. Either way it names a single person who acted, not a people.

decisions.choice: if God had not given it to you (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who is meant by "from above" (meaning decision m1) and uses "power" as in verse 10.

decisions.choice: carries the greater sin (B); is even more guilty of sin than you are (R)
decisions.reason: To "have sin" is a way of speaking of guilt, as in 9:41 and 15:22, 24. Readable says "even more ... than you are" to show that Pilate's own guilt is real (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἐκ τούτου ὁ Πιλᾶτος ἐζήτει ἀπολῦσαι αὐτόν· οἱ δὲ Ἰουδαῖοι ἐκραύγασαν λέγοντες· Ἐὰν τοῦτον ἀπολύσῃς, οὐκ εἶ φίλος τοῦ Καίσαρος· πᾶς ὁ βασιλέα ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν ἀντιλέγει τῷ Καίσαρι.
records.gloss: From this the Pilate was seeking to release him; but the Jews cried out saying, "If this [man] you release, not you are friend of the Caesar; everyone the king himself making speaks against the Caesar."

L.12: From this [time] Pilate was seeking to release Him, but the Jews shouted, saying, "If you release this [man], you are not a friend of Caesar; everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar."

R.12: After this, Pilate kept trying to find a way to let Jesus go. But the Jewish leaders shouted, "If you let this man go, you are not Caesar's friend! Anyone who says he is a king is an enemy of Caesar, the emperor!"

decisions.choice: from this: from then on, and because of what Jesus had said
decisions.reason: The phrase can mark time ("from then on") or a reason ("because of this"); John uses it the same way in 6:66, where both senses are possible. Here Jesus's answer is the turning point, so both fit.

decisions.choice: was seeking: kept trying
decisions.reason: The imperfect shows repeated or continued attempts. Pilate kept looking for a way to release Jesus, without success.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers, with those who stood with them outside the praetorium
decisions.reason: They are the accusers of verses 6-7, who answer Pilate again; in verse 15 John names the chief priests as the ones who speak for them. Others may have stood with them, as the shout for Barabbas suggests (18:39-40), but John does not describe a crowd. It is not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus and his disciples are Jews.

decisions.choice: Caesar's friend: loyal to the emperor, perhaps also an honored title
decisions.reason: "Caesar" here means the Roman emperor, Tiberius at this time (Luke 3:1). "Friend of Caesar" means one loyal to him; it was also used of men honored with the emperor's favor, but whether Pilate held such a title is not known. The threat is plain: if he releases a man accused of claiming to be king, they will report him as disloyal.

decisions.choice: makes himself a king speaks against Caesar: claims to be a king and so opposes the emperor
decisions.reason: The verb means to speak against and so to oppose; to set oneself up as a king in a Roman province was rebellion. "Makes himself a king" repeats the form of the charge in verse 7, "made himself the Son of God": the accusers now turn the religious charge into a political one.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: Caesar, the emperor (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says who Caesar was, the first time the name comes in the passage (meaning decision m4), and says "enemy of" for "speaks against" (meaning decision m5).

records.greek: Ὁ οὖν Πιλᾶτος ἀκούσας τῶν λόγων τούτων ἤγαγεν ἔξω τὸν Ἰησοῦν, καὶ ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ βήματος εἰς τόπον λεγόμενον Λιθόστρωτον, Ἑβραϊστὶ δὲ Γαββαθα.
records.gloss: The therefore Pilate, having heard the words these, brought outside the Jesus and sat on [the] judgment seat at a place called Stone Pavement, in Hebrew but Gabbatha.

L.13: So Pilate, having heard these words, brought Jesus outside and sat down on [the] judgment seat at a place called [the] Stone Pavement, but in Hebrew Gabbatha.

R.13: When Pilate heard this, he brought Jesus outside. He sat down on the judge's seat at a place called the Stone Pavement. In Hebrew its name was Gabbatha.

decisions.choice: sat down: Pilate took his seat
alternatives: Pilate seated Jesus on the judgment seat
decisions.reason: The verb usually means "sat" in John (12:14), and a governor sat on the judgment seat to give sentence (Matthew 27:19; Acts 25:6, 17). The verb can also mean "seated someone", and the sentence could then mean that Pilate set Jesus on the judgment seat in mockery, as the soldiers had dressed him as a king. That would fit John's irony, but without an object stated the plain sense is more likely.

decisions.choice: judgment seat: the raised platform where a Roman official sat to give his decision
decisions.reason: The word means a platform reached by steps. A Roman magistrate gave judgment from it in public (Acts 18:12; 25:6). By sitting there Pilate makes his decision formal.

decisions.choice: the Stone Pavement, in Hebrew Gabbatha: two names for the same place
decisions.reason: The first name means a floor laid with stones. "In Hebrew" means the language of the Jews of the land, which in daily speech was mostly Aramaic (as at 5:2). Gabbatha is not a translation of the first name; its meaning is uncertain, perhaps "height" or "raised place". The exact place in Jerusalem is not known.

decisions.choice: these words: the threat of verse 12
decisions.reason: It is the warning that he would be no friend of Caesar that moves Pilate to act.

decisions.choice: in Hebrew
decisions.reason: Keeps the word John used, as at 5:2; meaning decision m3 explains which language this was.

decisions.choice: the judge's seat (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what the seat was for (meaning decision m2) and breaks the long sentence.

records.greek: ἦν δὲ παρασκευὴ τοῦ πάσχα, ὥρα ἦν ὡς ἕκτη.
records.gloss: It was now Preparation of the Passover; hour was about sixth.

L.14: Now it was [the] Preparation of the Passover; it was about the sixth hour.

R.14: It was the day of Preparation, when people got ready for the Passover. The time was about noon.

decisions.choice: the Preparation of the Passover: the day before the Passover, when the meal was made ready
alternatives: the Friday of the Passover week
decisions.reason: On the day of preparation the Passover lambs were killed in the afternoon (Exodus 12:6) and the meal was eaten that evening, when the feast began. This fits 18:28, where the accusers have not yet eaten the Passover. The same word was also the name for Friday, the day of preparation before the Sabbath (19:31, 42; Mark 15:42), and some read it here as "the Friday of Passover week". Mark 14:12-16 presents the last supper as a Passover meal, so the two accounts need to be read together; the footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: about the sixth hour: about noon
alternatives: about six in the morning, counting from midnight
decisions.reason: Hours were counted from sunrise, about six in the morning (see the notes at 1:39 and 4:6), so the sixth hour was about midday. Mark 15:25 says Jesus was crucified at the third hour, about nine in the morning. Times of day were usually given loosely ("about"). Counting from midnight, which some have proposed for John, would give six in the morning. The difference is noted here, not settled.

decisions.choice: noon on the day of preparation: perhaps a link with the Passover lambs
alternatives: the time is given only as a fact
decisions.reason: At about this hour the preparations for killing the Passover lambs were beginning. John has called Jesus the Lamb of God (1:29, 36), and he will connect the Passover lamb with Jesus's death (19:36; Exodus 12:46). He does not draw the link here, so it is possible rather than certain.

decisions.choice: about the sixth hour (Literal); about noon (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for clock times in John: Literal keeps the hour as counted then, Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: the day of Preparation (B, R); when people got ready for the Passover (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "day". Readable says what the day was for (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: καὶ λέγει τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις· Ἴδε ὁ βασιλεὺς ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: And he says to the Jews, "See, the king of you!"

L.14: And he says to the Jews, "Look, your King!"

R.14: Pilate said to the Jewish leaders, "Look! Here is your King!"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers, with those who stood with them before the judgment seat
decisions.reason: Pilate speaks to the accusers of verses 6-12; in verse 15 John names the chief priests as the ones who answer. It is not the Jewish people as a whole. Yet Pilate addresses them as speaking for the nation, whose king he says Jesus is.

decisions.choice: Look, your King: Pilate's taunt, which John's reader knows to be true
decisions.reason: The words match verse 5, "Look, the man". Pilate mocks both the prisoner and those who accused him of claiming to be king. John's reader knows that Jesus is the King of Israel (1:49; 12:13-15) and that his kingdom is not from this world (18:36).

decisions.choice: he says: Pilate, seated on the judgment seat
decisions.reason: The subject is Pilate, who has just taken his seat (verse 13).

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: Pilate; here is (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker and say "here is", as in verse 5, so the two sayings are heard together.

records.greek: ἐκραύγασαν οὖν ἐκεῖνοι· Ἆρον ἆρον, σταύρωσον αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Cried out therefore those, "Take away, take away, crucify him!"

L.15: So those [men] shouted, "Take [Him] away, take [Him] away, crucify Him!"

R.15: But they shouted, "Take Him away! Take Him away! Crucify Him!"

decisions.choice: take away: remove him, that is, put him to death
alternatives: take him out of our sight
decisions.reason: The verb means to lift up and carry off. Shouted at a prisoner, it demands his removal by death, as in Luke 23:18 and Acts 22:22. The cry is doubled, as "Crucify, crucify" was in verse 6.

decisions.choice: those men: the ones Pilate has just addressed
decisions.reason: The pronoun points back to those of verse 14, and the next sentence names the chief priests as their spokesmen.

decisions.choice: Take [him] away (L); Away with him (B)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets "him", which the Greek leaves unstated; Balanced uses the English idiom for demanding someone's removal. Readable says "Take him away".

records.greek: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Τὸν βασιλέα ὑμῶν σταυρώσω;
records.gloss: Says to them the Pilate, "The king of you shall I crucify?"

L.15: Pilate says to them, "Shall I crucify your King?"

R.15: Pilate asked them, "Do you want me to crucify your King?"

decisions.choice: your King: placed first for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Greek begins with "your King": is it your own king that I am to crucify? The verb asks what he should do.

decisions.choice: your King: Pilate presses the taunt of verse 14
decisions.reason: Pilate holds them to the title. Whether he is mocking them or making one more attempt to release Jesus, he forces them to say what they will say next.

decisions.choice: Do you want me to crucify (R)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the question in a form young readers use. The emphasis on "your" is left to the voice.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς· Οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα εἰ μὴ Καίσαρα.
records.gloss: Answered the chief priests, "Not we have king except Caesar."

L.15: The chief priests answered, "We have no king except Caesar."

R.15: The leading priests answered, "The only king we have is Caesar!"

decisions.choice: the chief priests: John names these speakers
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Here John says who answered: the chief priests. The words are theirs, spoken as leaders before the governor; John does not put them in the mouth of the people.

decisions.choice: we have no king but Caesar: the irony of the chief priests' words
alternatives: a simple statement of political fact
decisions.reason: In Israel's Scriptures God himself is the King of his people (Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7; Isaiah 33:22), and Israel hoped for the Messiah, the King of Israel (1:49; 12:13). To press Pilate to act, the chief priests, who served God in his temple, say that they have no king but the emperor. John records the words without comment; the reader feels their weight.

decisions.choice: Caesar: the Roman emperor
decisions.reason: As in verse 12. In this period the high priest held office under Roman rule and was appointed by the Roman governor; the chief priests' position depended on Rome.

decisions.choice: The only king we have is Caesar (R); leading priests (R)
alternatives: We have no king but Caesar (Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the exception in a plain positive form; "leading priests" as in verse 6.

records.greek: τότε οὖν παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν αὐτοῖς ἵνα σταυρωθῇ.
records.gloss: Then therefore he handed over him to them that he might be crucified.

L.16: So then he handed Him over to them to be crucified.

R.16: So Pilate handed Jesus over to them to be crucified.

decisions.choice: to them: to the will of the chief priests, while Roman soldiers carried out the sentence
alternatives: handed him to the chief priests, who carried out the crucifixion
decisions.reason: By the grammar, "them" are the last people named, the chief priests (verse 15). Yet the crucifixion was carried out by Roman soldiers (19:23, 32), on the governor's order, and the charge set over the cross was Pilate's (19:19). So the sense is that Pilate gave Jesus up to what they demanded and handed him over for execution; it does not mean the chief priests crucified him themselves. Compare Luke 23:25, "he delivered Jesus over to their will". Every level keeps "to them" as the Greek has it.

decisions.choice: handed over: the same verb used all through the story
decisions.reason: Judas handed Jesus over (18:2, 5), the chief priests handed him over to Pilate (18:30, 35), and Jesus has spoken of the one who handed him over (19:11). Now Pilate, who has said three times that he finds no case against him, hands him over to be crucified. The responsibility for the sentence is the Roman governor's.

decisions.choice: Pilate (B, R); Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Pilate, since the last speakers were the chief priests. Readable names Jesus. "To them" stays at every level (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: Παρέλαβον οὖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν·
records.gloss: They took therefore the Jesus.

decisions.choice: they: those to whom Jesus was handed over; in fact the soldiers carried out the crucifixion
decisions.reason: John does not name the subject. It follows on from "them" in the sentence before, but the ones who crucified Jesus were the soldiers (19:23). This sentence opens the account of the crucifixion that follows.

decisions.choice: took: received him into their charge
decisions.reason: The verb means to take or receive someone from another. It is the word used in 1:11, "his own did not receive him"; whether John means the reader to hear that echo is uncertain.

decisions.choice: So they took Jesus (SBLGNT)
alternatives: They took Jesus and led him away (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "and led him away", and some have other short additions. The older manuscripts have the shorter text; the sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: took charge of (B)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that Jesus was received into custody (meaning decision m2).

records.heading: The crucifixion

records.greek: καὶ βαστάζων αὑτῷ τὸν σταυρὸν ἐξῆλθεν εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον Κρανίου Τόπον, ὃ λέγεται Ἑβραϊστὶ Γολγοθα, ὅπου αὐτὸν ἐσταύρωσαν, καὶ μετ’ αὐτοῦ ἄλλους δύο ἐντεῦθεν καὶ ἐντεῦθεν, μέσον δὲ τὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: And carrying for himself the cross he went out to the [place] being called Of-a-Skull Place, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha, \v 18 where him they crucified, and with him others two, on this side and on that side, and in the middle the Jesus.

L.17: And carrying the cross by Himself, He went out to the [place] called Place of a Skull, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha,
L.18: where they crucified Him, and with Him two others, on this side and on that side, and Jesus in the middle.

R.17: Jesus carried His own cross and went out of the city to a place called Skull Place. In the Hebrew language its name is Golgotha.
R.18: There the soldiers nailed Him to the cross. They also crucified two other men, one on each side of Jesus, so that Jesus was in the middle.

decisions.choice: carrying the cross by himself, with no one's help
alternatives: carrying the cross for his own sake
only that he set out carrying it, leaving open whether someone helped later
decisions.reason: The small word attached to "carrying" points back to Jesus: the cross was his own load. Matthew, Mark and Luke say the soldiers made Simon of Cyrene carry it (Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26). John does not mention Simon. The accounts can be read together (Jesus set out carrying it and Simon took it over on the way), but John's own telling shows Jesus carrying it himself.

decisions.choice: the cross: probably the crossbeam, which a condemned man carried to the place of execution
alternatives: the whole cross, upright and crossbeam
decisions.reason: Roman practice was for the condemned person to carry his cross to the place of execution, where the upright post often stood ready. What he carried was most likely the crossbeam, since a whole cross would have been too heavy for one man, especially one who had been flogged (19:1). John only says "the cross".

decisions.choice: Place of a Skull, in the local language Golgotha: John translates the name for his readers
decisions.reason: John gives the meaning of the name before the local name itself. "Hebrew" is John's word for the language of the Jews of the land, which in daily speech was mostly Aramaic, and Golgotha is the Aramaic word for "skull" (see 5:2; 19:13). Why it had that name is not known; it may have been the shape of the ground. The place was outside the city but near it (19:20; Hebrews 13:12).

decisions.choice: they crucified him: the Roman soldiers, as 19:23 says; and two others, whom John does not name
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject, and 19:16 says Pilate handed Jesus over "to them". But 19:23 says plainly that the soldiers crucified Jesus: crucifixion was a Roman penalty, carried out by Roman soldiers on the governor's order. John does not say who the other two men were; the other Gospels call them bandits or criminals (Mark 15:27; Luke 23:32-33).

decisions.choice: the soldiers nailed him to the cross (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the soldiers, from 19:23 (meaning decision m4), so that young readers do not take "they" to mean the last group mentioned. "Nailed" comes from the nail marks in 20:25 and explains the word "crucified" for readers who may not know it.

decisions.choice: Place of a Skull (L); the Place of the Skull (B); Skull Place (R); in Hebrew (every level)
decisions.reason: Each level gives John's own translation of the name. "Calvary" comes from the Latin word for skull and is not in the Greek. "Hebrew" keeps the word John used; meaning decision m3 explains which language this was.

records.greek: ἔγραψεν δὲ καὶ τίτλον ὁ Πιλᾶτος καὶ ἔθηκεν ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ· ἦν δὲ γεγραμμένον· Ἰησοῦς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
records.gloss: Wrote and also a title the Pilate and put [it] on the cross; was and written: Jesus the Nazorean the king of the Jews.

L.19: And Pilate also wrote a notice and put [it] on the cross; and it was written: "Jesus the Nazorean, the King of the Jews."

R.19: Pilate also wrote a sign and had it put on the cross. It said, "Jesus from Nazareth, the King of the Jews."

decisions.choice: a notice: a placard stating the charge, the Latin titulus
alternatives: an inscription carved on the cross
decisions.reason: The Greek word is the Latin "titulus", a board or placard with writing on it. Roman writers mention a placard naming a condemned person's crime, carried before him or hung on him; here it is fixed to the cross. The charge is the one Jesus was tried for: claiming to be a king (18:33-37; 19:12).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish nation, in the title of a king
decisions.reason: In "King of the Jews" the word names the people as a nation, as in Pilate's questions (18:33, 39) and the soldiers' mockery (19:3). It is the Roman charge against Jesus, in Pilate's words, and it is kept as written at every level.

decisions.choice: the charge is also true in John's telling: Jesus is the King of Israel
decisions.reason: Pilate meant the notice as the charge, perhaps with scorn for the people (19:15). John has already shown that Jesus is king in a sense Pilate did not grasp (1:49; 12:13-15; 18:36-37), so the notice says more than its writer intended, as Caiaphas's words did (11:50-52).

decisions.choice: Pilate wrote and put: he is responsible for the notice, whether or not his own hand did the work
alternatives: Pilate wrote it with his own hand
decisions.reason: A governor would normally have such a notice made and put up by others, and Greek often says that a person did what he had done. What matters to the story is that the wording is Pilate's, as he insists in 19:22.

decisions.choice: notice (L, B); sign (R); the Nazorean (L); of Nazareth (B); from Nazareth (R)
decisions.reason: "Title" now usually means the name of a book or a rank, so "notice" and "sign" say what the board was. Literal keeps the form of the word for Jesus's home town, which John uses (18:5, 7); Balanced and Readable say what it means.

records.greek: τοῦτον οὖν τὸν τίτλον πολλοὶ ἀνέγνωσαν τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ὅτι ἐγγὺς ἦν ὁ τόπος τῆς πόλεως ὅπου ἐσταυρώθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς· καὶ ἦν γεγραμμένον Ἑβραϊστί, Ῥωμαϊστί, Ἑλληνιστί.
records.gloss: This then the title many read of the Jews, because near was the place of the city where was crucified the Jesus; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, in Greek.

L.20: So many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, in Greek.

R.20: Many Jewish people from Jerusalem read the sign, because the place where Jesus hung on the cross was close to the city. The sign was written in three languages: Hebrew, Latin and Greek.

decisions.choice: the Jews: people of Jerusalem and the festival crowds who passed by
decisions.reason: Here the word means ordinary people who saw the notice because the place was near the city, at Passover when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims. The authorities appear separately in the next sentence as "the chief priests of the Jews".

decisions.choice: near the city: outside the walls, where many people would pass
decisions.reason: Executions took place outside the city (Leviticus 24:14; Numbers 15:35-36; Hebrews 13:12). The Romans crucified people where many would see them, as a warning, and John notes it to explain why so many read the notice.

decisions.choice: Hebrew, Latin, Greek: the local language, the language of Rome, and the common language of the eastern empire
decisions.reason: "Hebrew" is John's word for the language of the Jews of the land, mostly Aramaic in daily speech (19:17). The second word is literally "in Roman", meaning Latin, the language of the Roman government. Greek was spoken across the eastern Mediterranean. In all three languages the notice could be read by everyone in the city at the festival.

decisions.choice: Hebrew, Latin, Greek (SBLGNT)
alternatives: Hebrew, Greek, Latin (many later manuscripts; the King James Version follows this order)
decisions.reason: The manuscripts list the three languages in different orders. The order Hebrew, Latin, Greek is found in several early manuscripts; many later ones read Hebrew, Greek, Latin. The meaning is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Jews of Jerusalem (B); Jewish people from Jerusalem (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the people who were there (meaning decision m1), as in 8:48 and 10:31. "Jerusalem" is the city of this sentence ("near the city").

records.greek: ἔλεγον οὖν τῷ Πιλάτῳ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς τῶν Ἰουδαίων· Μὴ γράφε· Ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ἀλλ’ ὅτι ἐκεῖνος εἶπεν Βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων εἰμί.
records.gloss: Were saying then to the Pilate the chief priests of the Jews: Not write: The king of the Jews, but that that one said: King of the Jews I am.

L.21: So the chief priests of the Jews were saying to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but that that man said, 'I am King of the Jews.'"

R.21: So the chief priests of the Jews kept telling Pilate, "Do not write 'The King of the Jews.' Write that this man claimed to be King of the Jews."

decisions.choice: the chief priests of the Jews: the leading priests in Jerusalem, as heads of the nation
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Only here does John call them "the chief priests of the Jews". The phrase sets their title beside the one on the cross: the nation's chief priests object to the nation's king. It names the group that objected, the leading priests (18:35; 19:6, 15), not the people.

decisions.choice: were saying ... do not write: an objection pressed more than once, asking Pilate to change what he had put up
alternatives: a request made before the notice was written
decisions.reason: The verb of saying is in a tense that can describe a continuing or repeated action. The command "do not write" is in the present tense: Pilate had already written it (19:19), so they want the wording changed.

decisions.choice: that man said, 'I am King of the Jews': they want the title shown as his claim, not as fact
decisions.reason: The word for "that man" keeps Jesus at a distance, with contempt. As written, the notice states that he is the king; with their change it would only report his claim.

decisions.choice: objected ... they told Pilate (B); kept telling (R); Write that this man ... (B); claimed to be (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show the continuing objection with a verb English uses for it (meaning decision m2), and break the request into two sentences. Readable reports the claim indirectly to avoid quotation marks inside quotation marks.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Ὃ γέγραφα γέγραφα.
records.gloss: Answered the Pilate: What I have written, I have written.

L.22: Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."

R.22: Pilate answered, "What I have written will stay as I wrote it."

decisions.choice: What I have written, I have written: it stands and will not be changed
decisions.reason: Greek uses this tense for an action that is done and whose result remains. Saying it twice makes the answer final.

decisions.choice: Pilate's refusal: the governor will not let the priests change his notice
alternatives: Pilate refuses because he believes Jesus is a king
decisions.reason: John does not give Pilate's reason. The priests had just forced his hand (19:12-16), and the notice is a way of answering them. Pilate, who gave way on the sentence, does not give way on the wording, so the title stands over the cross.

decisions.choice: What I have written will stay as I wrote it (R)
alternatives: What I have written, I have written
decisions.reason: Readers new to the Bible may not hear a refusal in the repeated phrase, so Readable says what it means (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: οἱ οὖν στρατιῶται ὅτε ἐσταύρωσαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἔλαβον τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐποίησαν τέσσαρα μέρη, ἑκάστῳ στρατιώτῃ μέρος, καὶ τὸν χιτῶνα.
records.gloss: The then soldiers, when they crucified the Jesus, took the garments of him and made four parts, to each soldier a part, and the tunic.

L.23: Then the soldiers, when they crucified Jesus, took His garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and [took] the tunic.

R.23: After the soldiers had nailed Jesus to the cross, they took His clothes and split them into four parts, one part for each soldier. They also took His tunic, the long shirt He wore next to His skin.

decisions.choice: four soldiers: a Roman squad of four carried out the crucifixion
decisions.reason: Roman soldiers often worked in groups of four (compare Acts 12:4). The clothes of a person being executed were usually taken by those who carried out the sentence. The sentence names the Roman soldiers plainly as the ones who crucified Jesus.

decisions.choice: garments: his outer clothing (cloak, belt, sandals and the like); tunic: the long shirt worn next to the skin
alternatives: garments and tunic as two words for the same clothing
decisions.reason: The plural word for garments means outer clothes in general. The tunic was the inner garment, a long shirt reaching to the knees or ankles, worn under the cloak. John sets the tunic apart because of what happens to it next.

decisions.choice: garments (L); clothes (B, R); tunic at every level, explained at Readable
decisions.reason: "Tunic" is the exact word for the long inner shirt; "coat" or "robe" would suggest an outer garment. Readable adds a short description for young readers.

records.greek: ἦν δὲ ὁ χιτὼν ἄραφος, ἐκ τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑφαντὸς δι’ ὅλου·
records.gloss: Was now the tunic seamless, from the top woven through whole.

L.23: Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top through the whole.

R.23: This tunic had no seams. It was woven in one piece, from the top all the way down.

decisions.choice: from the top: woven from the top down, in one piece
decisions.reason: John uses the same word elsewhere for "from above" (3:31; 19:11), and "again, from above" (3:3, 7). Here it describes the weaving, from the neck down, with no seam.

decisions.choice: the detail explains why the soldiers did not tear it; John may also see more in it
alternatives: a sign that Jesus is high priest, whose robe was woven without a seam
a picture of the unity of Jesus's people, who are not to be torn apart
decisions.reason: The plain reason for the detail is the next sentence: a seamless tunic was worth more whole. Two further meanings have been proposed. The high priest's robe was to be woven so that it would not tear (Exodus 28:32), and the Jewish historian Josephus says it was not made of two pieces but woven in one. And the word "tear" (19:24) is the word John uses for divisions among people (7:43; 9:16; 10:19) and for the net that was not torn (21:11). John does not say that he means either, so this is uncertain.

decisions.choice: in a single piece from top to bottom (B); in one piece, from the top all the way down (R)
decisions.reason: "Through the whole" means it was woven all in one; Balanced and Readable say so plainly.

records.greek: εἶπαν οὖν πρὸς ἀλλήλους· Μὴ σχίσωμεν αὐτόν, ἀλλὰ λάχωμεν περὶ αὐτοῦ τίνος ἔσται· ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ ἡ λέγουσα· Διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτιά μου ἑαυτοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμόν μου ἔβαλον κλῆρον.
records.gloss: They said then to one another: Not let us tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it will be; so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, the [one] saying: They divided the garments of me among themselves, and for the clothing of me they cast a lot.

L.24: So they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, [to see] whose it will be," so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says, "They divided My garments among themselves, and for My clothing they cast a lot."

R.24: So the soldiers said to each other, "Let us not tear it. Let us draw lots to see who will get it." This happened to make the Scripture come true that says, "They divided My clothes among themselves, and they drew lots for My clothing."

decisions.choice: cast lots: a game of chance to decide who would have it
decisions.reason: Lots were marked stones or pieces of bone, thrown or drawn to decide a matter. Soldiers also played with dice. Either way, chance decided which soldier kept the tunic whole.

decisions.choice: Psalm 22:19, quoted word for word from the Greek translation of the psalm
decisions.reason: The words are those of Psalm 22:19 in the Greek translation used in John's day, which follows the Hebrew closely. The psalm is the prayer of a righteous sufferer, surrounded by enemies, who is rescued by God; its first line is Jesus's cry in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34. John uses it to show that what the soldiers did was foretold.

decisions.choice: John reads the psalm's two lines as two acts: the garments divided, the tunic given by lot
alternatives: the two lines say one thing twice, as Hebrew poetry often does
decisions.reason: In the psalm the two lines are parallel and describe one act. John's account matches each line to a separate deed: the soldiers divide the outer garments (19:23) and cast lots for the tunic.

decisions.choice: so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: the narrator's comment on God's purpose, not the soldiers' aim
alternatives: the soldiers acted in order to fulfill Scripture
decisions.reason: The soldiers knew nothing of the psalm. John's formula (12:38; 13:18; 15:25; 19:36) says that what happened was in keeping with what God had said beforehand.

decisions.choice: This was so that ... (B); This happened to make ... come true (R)
alternatives: so that the Scripture might be fulfilled (Literal, joined to the soldiers' words)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable start a new sentence for John's comment so that it is not read as part of what the soldiers said (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: draw lots (R); cast lots (L, B)
decisions.reason: "Draw lots" is the plainer phrase for young readers and keeps the sense of chance without naming a game the text does not name.

records.greek: Οἱ μὲν οὖν στρατιῶται ταῦτα ἐποίησαν.
records.gloss: The on the one hand then soldiers these things did.

L.24: So the soldiers did these things.

R.24: So that is what the soldiers did.

decisions.choice: a closing line that sets the soldiers against the women in the next sentence
decisions.reason: The small word in this sentence, answered by another in the next (19:25), sets the two scenes side by side: on one side the soldiers dividing his clothes, on the other the women and the disciple standing by the cross.

decisions.choice: That is what the soldiers did (B); So that is what the soldiers did (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the sentence sound like the close of the scene, which is its job in the Greek (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: Εἱστήκεισαν δὲ παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ ἀδελφὴ τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ, Μαρία ἡ τοῦ Κλωπᾶ καὶ Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή.
records.gloss: Had stood now by the cross of the Jesus the mother of him and the sister of the mother of him, Mary the [one] of Clopas, and Mary the Magdalene.

L.25: But standing by the cross of Jesus were His mother and His mother's sister, Mary the [wife] of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

R.25: Some women were standing near the cross of Jesus. They were His mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

decisions.choice: four women: his mother, his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
alternatives: three women: his mother's sister is Mary the wife of Clopas
two women: his mother and her sister, named as the two Marys
decisions.reason: The Greek has no "and" between "his mother's sister" and "Mary of Clopas", so they could be the same woman. But then two sisters would both be called Mary, which is unlikely. Read as four, the list falls into two pairs joined by "and": two women not named, then two named Marys. The evidence is not decisive.

decisions.choice: Mary the wife of Clopas
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "Mary of Clopas", a way of naming a woman by a man she belonged to, most often her husband, sometimes her father or son. "Wife" is the usual sense. Nothing more is known of Clopas; whether he is the Cleopas of Luke 24:18 is uncertain.

decisions.choice: Magdalene: from Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee
decisions.reason: Mary Magdalene is named here for the first time in John; she is the first to find the tomb empty and to see the risen Jesus (20:1-18). Luke 8:2 says Jesus had freed her from seven demons.

decisions.choice: his mother's sister: John does not name her
decisions.reason: Other Gospels name women at the cross: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome or the mother of Zebedee's sons (Matthew 27:56; Mark 15:40). Whether John's unnamed sister of Jesus's mother is one of these cannot be known from the text.

decisions.choice: Meanwhile (B); Some women were standing (R)
decisions.reason: The sentence turns from the soldiers to the people who loved Jesus (19:24 meaning decision m1). Balanced marks the turn with "Meanwhile"; Readable starts with the women and then lists them, without saying how many (meaning decision m1).

records.heading: Jesus's mother at the cross

records.greek: Ἰησοῦς οὖν ἰδὼν τὴν μητέρα καὶ τὸν μαθητὴν παρεστῶτα ὃν ἠγάπα λέγει τῇ μητρί· Γύναι, ἴδε ὁ υἱός σου·
records.gloss: Jesus then, having seen the mother and the disciple standing by whom he loved, says to the mother: Woman, behold the son of you.

L.26: So Jesus, seeing His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing by, says to His mother, "Woman, look, your son."

R.26: Jesus saw His mother there. The disciple whom He loved was standing near her. Jesus said to His mother, "Mother, he is your son now."

decisions.choice: Woman: a respectful address, as at Cana
decisions.reason: Jesus uses this address to his mother only twice, at Cana (2:4) and here. At Cana he said, "My hour has not yet come"; now his hour has come (12:23; 13:1; 17:1), and at the cross he speaks to her again in the same way. The address was courteous, not rude.

decisions.choice: look, your son: a declaration that makes a new bond, the disciple to be her son
alternatives: only pointing out the disciple standing there
decisions.reason: The words do not simply point at someone; they give the disciple to her as a son, and the next sentence gives her to him as a mother. The disciple acts on it at once (19:27).

decisions.choice: a dying son's care for his mother; perhaps also the start of a new family of his disciples
alternatives: chiefly a symbol, with the mother standing for a people of faith
decisions.reason: The first sense is plain: Jesus makes sure his mother will be cared for. His brothers did not yet believe in him (7:5). John may also mean more: from the cross Jesus joins his mother and his disciple as one family, and after the resurrection he calls his disciples "my brothers" (20:17). The text does not say so directly.

decisions.choice: the disciple whom Jesus loved: the disciple John does not name
decisions.reason: This disciple first appears at the last supper (13:23) and stands at the cross when the other disciples have scattered (16:32). The Gospel says he is the source of its witness (19:35; 21:24).

decisions.choice: said (B, R); says (L), and so through this passage (19:27, 19:28)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English normally tells a story. This applies to every such verb in this passage.

decisions.choice: Woman
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "Woman" so that readers can connect this scene with Cana (2:4); the footnote on meaning decision m1 says the address was respectful. "Dear woman" would add warmth the word does not carry on its own.

decisions.choice: Mother, he is your son now (R)
decisions.reason: For young readers "Woman" sounds rude, which the Greek is not. She is his mother, so Readable uses the address a son would use, as it does at 2:4. "Now" shows that the words make a new bond (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: εἶτα λέγει τῷ μαθητῇ· Ἴδε ἡ μήτηρ σου.
records.gloss: Then he says to the disciple: Behold the mother of you.

L.27: Then He says to the disciple, "Look, your mother."

R.27: Then He said to the disciple, "She is your mother now."

decisions.choice: look, your mother: the other half of the declaration in 19:26
decisions.reason: The two sayings match: she is to be his mother, and he is to be her son. Together they put her in the disciple's care as a son cares for his mother.

decisions.choice: She is your mother now (R)
decisions.reason: As in 19:26, Readable says what the words do, giving the disciple a mother to care for.

records.greek: καὶ ἀπ’ ἐκείνης τῆς ὥρας ἔλαβεν ὁ μαθητὴς αὐτὴν εἰς τὰ ἴδια.
records.gloss: And from that the hour took the disciple her into the own [things].

L.27: And from that hour the disciple took her into his own [home].

R.27: From then on, that disciple took her to live in his home.

decisions.choice: from that hour: from that time on, starting then
alternatives: from Jesus's appointed hour, meaning the cross as the hour of his glory
decisions.reason: Here "hour" means a time of day: the disciple acted at once. But John has spoken of Jesus's hour throughout the Gospel (2:4; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1), and at the cross that hour has come, so the word may also remind readers of it.

decisions.choice: into his own: into his own home, as one of his household
alternatives: into his own care, without saying where she lived
decisions.reason: "His own" is a common way of saying "his home" or "his own people" (1:11; 16:32). Taking her into it means more than a place to stay: she became part of his household.

decisions.choice: From that time on (B); From then on (R); from that hour (L)
decisions.reason: Here "hour" is a time of day, not Jesus's appointed hour (which Balanced writes as "hour"), so Balanced and Readable say "time". Literal keeps "hour" so that the possible echo can be seen (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: Μετὰ τοῦτο εἰδὼς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤδη πάντα τετέλεσται ἵνα τελειωθῇ ἡ γραφὴ λέγει· Διψῶ.
records.gloss: After this, knowing the Jesus that already all things have been finished, so that might be completed the Scripture, says: I thirst.

L.28: After this, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been finished, so that the Scripture might be completed, says, "I thirst."

R.28: After this, Jesus knew that everything He had come to do was now finished. To make the Scripture come fully true, He said, "I am thirsty."

decisions.choice: so that the Scripture might be completed goes with "he says": he said "I thirst" to fulfill the Scripture
alternatives: it goes with "all things had been finished": everything was done so that the Scripture would be completed
decisions.reason: The purpose clause stands between the two verbs and could belong to either. Joined to "he says", it explains the saying by the Scripture about thirst (meaning decision m3), as 19:24 and 19:36 explain other details. Joined to "finished", it would say that the whole work was done to complete the Scripture, and "I thirst" would be simply his need. Both readings are possible.

decisions.choice: finished ... completed: the work the Father gave Jesus is done; the Scripture is brought to completion
decisions.reason: The first verb is the one Jesus says in 19:30, "It is finished". The second is not John's usual word for fulfilling Scripture (19:24) but the word Jesus used for completing the Father's work (4:34; 5:36; 17:4). John uses it to show that the Scripture, like the work, has reached its goal.

decisions.choice: I thirst: Psalm 69:22, with Psalm 22:16 in the background
alternatives: only a statement of physical thirst, with no Scripture in mind
decisions.reason: Psalm 69:22 says "for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink", and the next verse in John has the sour wine. Psalm 22, already quoted in 19:24, says "my tongue sticks to my jaws" (22:16). Both psalms are prayers of the righteous sufferer. The thirst was real: he had been flogged and had hung on the cross for hours.

decisions.choice: knowing: Jesus goes to his death aware and in control
decisions.reason: John often says what Jesus knew at turning points of the passion (13:1, 3; 18:4). He lays down his life of his own accord (10:18), and he speaks this word knowing that his work is now done.

decisions.choice: finished (as in 19:30); completed (as in 17:4); I thirst (L); I am thirsty (B, R)
alternatives: I am thirsty at every level
decisions.reason: "Finished" is the same English word as Jesus's last saying (19:30), and "completed" the same as "having completed the work" in 17:4, so the links in the Greek stay visible (meaning decision m2). Readable says what had been finished, from 17:4.

records.heading: The death of Jesus

records.greek: σκεῦος ἔκειτο ὄξους μεστόν· σπόγγον οὖν μεστὸν τοῦ ὄξους ὑσσώπῳ περιθέντες προσήνεγκαν αὐτοῦ τῷ στόματι.
records.gloss: A vessel was lying of sour wine full; a sponge then full of the sour wine on hyssop having put around, they brought [it] to him the mouth.

L.29: A jar full of sour wine was standing [there]; so, putting a sponge full of the sour wine on hyssop, they brought [it] to His mouth.

R.29: A jar of sour wine was sitting nearby. So they soaked a sponge in it, put the sponge on the end of a hyssop stick, and lifted it up to His mouth.

decisions.choice: sour wine: cheap wine gone sour, the everyday drink of soldiers and laborers
alternatives: drugged wine offered to dull pain
decisions.reason: The word means wine that has turned sour, which mixed with water was a common drink for soldiers and workers. It is the word in the Greek of Psalm 69:22 (see 19:28). Giving it may have been simple relief rather than mockery; John does not say. It is not the wine mixed with myrrh that Mark says Jesus refused before he was crucified (Mark 15:23).

decisions.choice: hyssop: the plant used to put the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts
alternatives: only the nearest plant stem, with no further meaning
decisions.reason: Hyssop is a small, bushy plant. Israel used a bunch of it to put the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorframes (Exodus 12:22), and it was used in cleansing (Leviticus 14:4; Psalm 51:9). John has told the story so that Jesus dies on the day the Passover lambs are killed (18:28; 19:14) and calls him the Lamb of God (1:29); he applies a Passover rule to him in 19:36. The mention of hyssop most likely points to this.

decisions.choice: on hyssop (all manuscripts)
alternatives: on a javelin: a guess, found in one late manuscript, that a similar word for the Roman javelin (in Latin, pilum) stood here
decisions.reason: A stalk of hyssop seems too weak to lift a soaked sponge, so it has been suggested that John wrote a very similar word meaning "javelin", and that a copyist misread it. The guess appears in only one late manuscript, of about the eleventh century; all the early manuscripts read "hyssop". A small branch would be enough, since a cross was often not much higher than a man. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they: the people standing by the cross, most likely the soldiers
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. The soldiers are the last group said to act (19:23-24), and sour wine was their drink, so they are the most likely ones.

decisions.choice: jar; sour wine; hyssop (L); a stalk of hyssop (B); a hyssop stick (R)
decisions.reason: "Vinegar" today means something no one drinks; "sour wine" says what it was (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable say what part of the plant was used. Every level keeps "hyssop" so the Passover link can be seen (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ὅτε οὖν ἔλαβεν τὸ ὄξος ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Τετέλεσται, καὶ κλίνας τὴν κεφαλὴν παρέδωκεν τὸ πνεῦμα.
records.gloss: When then took the sour wine the Jesus, he said: It has been finished, and having bowed the head he handed over the spirit.

L.30: So when Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, "It is finished," and bowing His head, He handed over His spirit.

R.30: Jesus drank the sour wine and said, "It is finished." Then He bowed His head, handed over His spirit, and died.

decisions.choice: It is finished: the work is completed, carried through to its goal, and it stands
alternatives: it is over: his life has ended
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring something to its end or goal. It is the word of 19:28, and it answers Jesus's words about completing the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4) and loving his own "to the end" (13:1). The tense means a thing done whose result remains. It is a cry of completion, not of defeat.

decisions.choice: handed over his spirit: he died, giving up his life himself
alternatives: breathed his last, with nothing more meant
decisions.reason: "To give up the spirit" is a way of saying someone died, and "spirit" here is his own life and breath, as in Luke 23:46. John's verb is the one used all through the passion for handing someone over (Judas, 18:2, 5; the chief priests, 18:30, 35; Pilate, 19:16). Now Jesus hands over his own life: no one takes it from him (10:18).

decisions.choice: his own spirit; John may also hint that the Spirit is now to be given
alternatives: a plain statement that he died, with no reference to the Holy Spirit
he handed over the Holy Spirit to those at the cross
decisions.reason: John said the Spirit would be given once Jesus was glorified (7:39), and the risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and gives them the Holy Spirit (20:22). Some read a hint of that here, since the words could also mean "handed over the Spirit". But the phrase is a natural way to describe death, and the Spirit is given in 20:22. The sense "his own spirit" is certain; a further hint is possible but not clear.

decisions.choice: bowing his head: first he bowed his head, then he died
decisions.reason: The order of the words shows the order of events: Jesus bows his head and then hands over his spirit, as one who chooses the moment.

decisions.choice: It is finished (every level); handed over his spirit, with "spirit" in lowercase
decisions.reason: "Finished" is the word used in 19:28, so the link stays visible. "Handed over" keeps the verb John uses throughout the passion (meaning decision m2). "Spirit" is lowercase because it is his own spirit (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: and died (R)
decisions.reason: Young readers may not know that "handed over his spirit" means that he died, so Readable says it plainly.

records.greek: Οἱ οὖν Ἰουδαῖοι, ἐπεὶ παρασκευὴ ἦν, ἵνα μὴ μείνῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὰ σώματα ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ, ἦν γὰρ μεγάλη ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνου τοῦ σαββάτου, ἠρώτησαν τὸν Πιλᾶτον ἵνα κατεαγῶσιν αὐτῶν τὰ σκέλη καὶ ἀρθῶσιν.
records.gloss: The therefore Jews, since Preparation it was, so that not might remain on the cross the bodies on the Sabbath, was for great the day of that the Sabbath, asked the Pilate that might be broken of them the legs and they might be taken away.

L.31: So the Jews, since it was [the] Preparation, so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for the day of that Sabbath was a great [one]), asked Pilate that their legs be broken and [that] they be taken away.

R.31: It was the day of Preparation, when people got everything ready for the Sabbath. The Jewish leaders did not want the bodies left on the crosses on the Sabbath, because that Sabbath was a very special day. So they asked Pilate to have the legs of the men broken, so that they would die sooner, and to have the bodies taken down.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the authorities, the chief priests and those with them
decisions.reason: They act as a body and make a formal request of the Roman governor, as the chief priests and their officers did throughout the trial (18:28-31; 19:6-7, 12, 15, 21). It is not the people as a whole: Jesus, his disciples, and Joseph and Nicodemus, who bury him, are Jews.

decisions.choice: Preparation: the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday
alternatives: the day before the Passover only
decisions.reason: The word means preparation, and it was the ordinary name for the sixth day of the week, when food was cooked and everything made ready so that no work need be done on the Sabbath (Mark 15:42 calls it "the day before the Sabbath"). John has called this day "the Preparation of the Passover" (19:14); in his account the Passover meal was still to be eaten that evening (18:28). The Sabbath began at sunset, so the time was short.

decisions.choice: so that the bodies would not remain on the cross: to keep the law about the body of an executed man
decisions.reason: The law said that the body of a man hanged on a tree must not stay there overnight but must be buried the same day, so as not to defile the land (Deuteronomy 21:22-23; compare Joshua 8:29; 10:26-27). The coming Sabbath made the matter more pressing. The Romans often left the crucified on their crosses for days; the request asks the governor to set that aside. "The cross" is singular in the Greek but speaks of each cross: three men were crucified (19:18).

decisions.choice: a great day: that Sabbath was also a feast day of Passover week
alternatives: only that every Sabbath was holy
decisions.reason: John has said that the Passover meal was to be eaten that evening (18:28; 19:14), so the Sabbath that followed was also the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, a day of holy assembly (Leviticus 23:6-7). A Sabbath that fell on a feast day was doubly holy. The Greek says literally "great was the day of that Sabbath".

decisions.choice: that their legs be broken and they be taken away: to bring death sooner, so that the bodies could be taken down before the Sabbath
decisions.reason: Breaking the legs of the crucified was a known Roman practice. A crucified man with broken legs could no longer push himself up to breathe, and so he died soon after. "Taken away" means removed from the cross for burial; the same verb is used of Joseph taking the body in verse 38.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: It was the day of Preparation ... because that Sabbath was a day of special importance (B); a very special day (R)
